name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q01 - Volume of hydrogen gas from reaction of ethanol with sodium

questiontext.text:
What volume of dihydrogen gas (\(\mathrm{H_2}\)) at STP is evolved when \(4.6\text{ g}\) of pure ethanol (\(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH}\)) reacts completely with excess sodium metal?

(Take molar mass of \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} = 46\text{ g mol}^{-1}\) and molar volume of an ideal gas at STP \(= 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of ethanol (\(m\)) \(= 4.6\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of ethanol (\(M\)) \(= 46\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar volume of gas at STP \(= 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\).
The reaction occurs with excess sodium metal to completion.

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Ethanol behaves as a weak Brønsted acid releasing acidic hydrogen upon reduction by sodium.
Hydrogen gas behaves ideally under standard temperature and pressure (STP).

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
The balanced chemical equation is:
\[2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + 2\,\mathrm{Na} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5ONa} + \mathrm{H_2}\]
Number of moles \(n = \frac{m}{M}\).
Moles of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) produced: \(n_{\mathrm{H_2}} = \frac{1}{2} n_{\mathrm{ethanol}}\).
Volume of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) at STP: \(V = n_{\mathrm{H_2}} \times 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate moles of ethanol:
\[n_{\mathrm{ethanol}} = \frac{4.6\text{ g}}{46\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.10\text{ mol}\]
2. Relate moles of ethanol to moles of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) from the stoichiometric coefficients:
\[n_{\mathrm{H_2}} = \frac{0.10\text{ mol}}{2} = 0.05\text{ mol}\]
3. Compute volume of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas at STP:
\[V_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 0.05\text{ mol} \times 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1} = 1.12\text{ L}\]

Check and Final Answer:
Since \(2\text{ moles}\) of alcohol yield \(1\text{ mole}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas, \(0.1\text{ mole}\) of alcohol yields \(0.05\text{ mole}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2}\), which equals \(1.12\text{ L}\) at STP. The calculation is dimensionally consistent and matches stoichiometric proportions.
The final answer is \(1.12\text{ L}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q02 - Mass of methanol formed in catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide

questiontext.text:
Methanol is industrially manufactured by the catalytic hydrogenation of carbon monoxide in the presence of a \(\mathrm{ZnO}-\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}\) catalyst:

\[\mathrm{CO(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{ZnO}-\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}} \mathrm{CH_3OH(l)}\]

If \(56\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{CO}\) reacts with \(10\text{ g}\) of \(\mathrm{H_2}\), what is the maximum mass of methanol (\(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\)) that can be formed?

(Take molar masses: \(\mathrm{CO} = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{H_2} = 2.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3OH} = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of \(\mathrm{CO} = 56\text{ g}\).
Mass of \(\mathrm{H_2} = 10\text{ g}\).
Molar masses: \(M_{\mathrm{CO}} = 28\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(M_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 2.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(M_{\mathrm{CH_3OH}} = 32\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The reaction goes to completion limited by whichever reactant is the limiting reagent.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Chemical equation: \[\mathrm{CO} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3OH}\]
Moles of reactant: \(n = \frac{m}{M}\).
Limiting reagent comparison: Compare \(\frac{n_{\mathrm{CO}}}{1}\) and \(\frac{n_{\mathrm{H_2}}}{2}\).
Theoretical yield of \(\mathrm{CH_3OH} = n_{\text{limiting}} \times M_{\mathrm{CH_3OH}}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate initial moles of each reactant:
\[n_{\mathrm{CO}} = \frac{56\text{ g}}{28\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 2.0\text{ mol}\]
\[n_{\mathrm{H_2}} = \frac{10\text{ g}}{2.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 5.0\text{ mol}\]
2. Determine the limiting reagent:
According to stoichiometry, \(1\text{ mol of CO}\) requires \(2\text{ mol of } \mathrm{H_2}\).
For \(2.0\text{ mol of CO}\), the required \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is \(2.0 \times 2 = 4.0\text{ mol}\).
Since \(5.0\text{ mol of } \mathrm{H_2}\) is available, \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is in excess and \(\mathrm{CO}\) is the limiting reagent.
3. Calculate mass of methanol produced:
\[n_{\mathrm{CH_3OH}} = n_{\mathrm{CO}} = 2.0\text{ mol}\]
\[m_{\mathrm{CH_3OH}} = 2.0\text{ mol} \times 32\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 64\text{ g}\]

Check and Final Answer:
Total mass of reactants reacted \(= 56\text{ g (CO)} + 8\text{ g (H}_2) = 64\text{ g}\), satisfying conservation of mass.
The final answer is \(64\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q03 - Dihydrogen evolved from tert-butyl alcohol and aluminium

questiontext.text:
When tert-butyl alcohol (\(\mathrm{2\text{-methylpropan-2-ol}}\)) reacts with aluminium metal, aluminium tert-butoxide and dihydrogen gas are formed according to the reaction:

\[6\,(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-OH} + 2\,\mathrm{Al} \rightarrow 2\,[(\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O}]_3\mathrm{Al} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2}\]

What volume of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas at STP will be liberated when \(22.2\text{ g}\) of tert-butyl alcohol reacts completely with excess aluminium?

(Take molar mass of tert-butyl alcohol \(= 74\text{ g mol}^{-1}\) and molar volume of gas at STP \(= 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of tert-butyl alcohol \(= 22.2\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of tert-butyl alcohol, \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{COH} = 4 \times 12 + 10 \times 1 + 16 = 74\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar volume of ideal gas at STP \(= 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\).
Aluminium is present in excess.

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The reaction goes to completion following the stoichiometry of the balanced chemical equation.
The liberated \(\mathrm{H_2}\) gas behaves ideally at STP.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Stoichiometric ratio: \(6\text{ moles of } (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{COH}\) produce \(3\text{ moles of } \mathrm{H_2}\).
Thus, \(n_{\mathrm{H_2}} = \frac{3}{6} n_{\text{alcohol}} = \frac{1}{2} n_{\text{alcohol}}\).
Volume of gas at STP: \(V = n \times 22.4\text{ L}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate moles of tert-butyl alcohol reacted:
\[n_{\text{alcohol}} = \frac{22.2\text{ g}}{74\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.30\text{ mol}\]
2. Calculate moles of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) generated:
\[n_{\mathrm{H_2}} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.30\text{ mol} = 0.15\text{ mol}\]
3. Calculate volume of \(\mathrm{H_2}\) at STP:
\[V_{\mathrm{H_2}} = 0.15\text{ mol} \times 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1} = 3.36\text{ L}\]

Check and Final Answer:
Since \(0.3\text{ mol}\) of a monohydric alcohol contains \(0.3\text{ mol}\) of acidic protons, they combine to form \(0.15\text{ mol}\) of diatomic \(\mathrm{H_2}\) molecules. Multiplying by \(22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\) yields \(3.36\text{ L}\).
The final answer is \(3.36\text{ L}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q04 - Mass of bromine required for complete tribromination of phenol

questiontext.text:
When phenol is treated with bromine water, a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol is formed quantitatively:

\[\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\,\mathrm{Br_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3OH} + 3\,\mathrm{HBr}\]

What minimum mass of bromine (\(\mathrm{Br_2}\)) in grams is required to completely convert \(14.1\text{ g}\) of phenol into 2,4,6-tribromophenol?

(Take atomic masses: \(\mathrm{C} = 12\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{H} = 1\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{O} = 16\text{ u}\), \(\mathrm{Br} = 80\text{ u}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of phenol \(= 14.1\text{ g}\).
Atomic masses: \(\mathrm{C} = 12\), \(\mathrm{H} = 1\), \(\mathrm{O} = 16\), \(\mathrm{Br} = 80\).
Molar mass of phenol (\(\mathrm{C_6H_6O}\)): \(6 \times 12 + 6 \times 1 + 16 = 94\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar mass of bromine (\(\mathrm{Br_2}\)): \(2 \times 80 = 160\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The reaction goes to completion with 100% conversion to the 2,4,6-tribromo derivative in aqueous medium due to strong activation of the ring by the phenoxide/hydroxyl group.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Balanced equation: \[\mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + 3\,\mathrm{Br_2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_2Br_3OH} + 3\,\mathrm{HBr}\]
Mole ratio: \(1\text{ mole of phenol}\) reacts with \(3\text{ moles of } \mathrm{Br_2}\).
\(n_{\text{phenol}} = \frac{m_{\text{phenol}}}{M_{\text{phenol}}}\).
\(m_{\mathrm{Br_2}} = n_{\mathrm{Br_2}} \times M_{\mathrm{Br_2}} = (3 \times n_{\text{phenol}}) \times 160\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate moles of phenol:
\[n_{\text{phenol}} = \frac{14.1\text{ g}}{94\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.15\text{ mol}\]
2. Calculate moles of \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) required:
\[n_{\mathrm{Br_2}} = 3 \times 0.15\text{ mol} = 0.45\text{ mol}\]
3. Calculate mass of \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) needed:
\[m_{\mathrm{Br_2}} = 0.45\text{ mol} \times 160\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 72.0\text{ g}\]

Check and Final Answer:
Ratio of mass of \(\mathrm{Br_2}\) to phenol is \(\frac{3 \times 160}{94} = \frac{480}{94} \approx 5.106\).
Multiplying \(14.1\text{ g}\) by \(5.106\) gives \(72.0\text{ g}\). The calculation is verified.
The final answer is \(72.0\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q05 - Mass of salicylic acid required to produce aspirin

questiontext.text:
Acetylation of salicylic acid with acetic anhydride produces acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) according to the equation:

\[\mathrm{C_7H_6O_3} + (\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_9H_8O_4} + \mathrm{CH_3COOH}\]

If the reaction proceeds with an \(80\%\) percentage yield, what mass of salicylic acid (\(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_3}\)) is required to produce \(36.0\text{ g}\) of pure aspirin?

(Take molar masses: Salicylic acid \(= 138\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), Aspirin \(= 180\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Actual mass of aspirin produced \(= 36.0\text{ g}\).
Percentage yield \(= 80\%\).
Molar mass of salicylic acid (\(\mathrm{C_7H_6O_3}\)) \(= 138\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar mass of aspirin (\(\mathrm{C_9H_8O_4}\)) \(= 180\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Salicylic acid is the limiting reactant.
Percentage yield is defined as \(\frac{\text{Actual yield}}{\text{Theoretical yield}} \times 100\%\).

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Stoichiometry: \(1\text{ mol of salicylic acid}\) theoretically yields \(1\text{ mol of aspirin}\).
Theoretical mass of aspirin \(= \frac{\text{Actual mass}}{\text{Yield}} = \frac{36.0\text{ g}}{0.80}\).
Theoretical moles of aspirin: \(n_{\text{theoretical}} = \frac{m_{\text{theoretical}}}{M_{\text{aspirin}}}\).
Mass of salicylic acid: \(m = n_{\text{theoretical}} \times M_{\text{salicylic acid}}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate the theoretical mass of aspirin needed:
\[m_{\text{aspirin (theoretical)}} = \frac{36.0\text{ g}}{0.80} = 45.0\text{ g}\]
2. Calculate the theoretical moles of aspirin:
\[n = \frac{45.0\text{ g}}{180\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.25\text{ mol}\]
3. From 1:1 stoichiometry, moles of salicylic acid required \(= 0.25\text{ mol}\).
4. Calculate the required mass of salicylic acid:
\[m_{\text{salicylic acid}} = 0.25\text{ mol} \times 138\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 34.5\text{ g}\]

Check and Final Answer:
At 100% yield, \(27.6\text{ g}\) of salicylic acid would give \(36.0\text{ g}\) of aspirin. At 80% yield, the required mass must be greater: \(\frac{27.6\text{ g}}{0.80} = 34.5\text{ g}\).
The final answer is \(34.5\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q06 - Volume of carbon dioxide released in fermentation of glucose

questiontext.text:
Ethanol is commercially prepared by the fermentation of sugars. Glucose undergoes conversion into ethanol and carbon dioxide in the presence of the enzyme zymase:

\[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} \xrightarrow{\text{zymase}} 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + 2\,\mathrm{CO_2}\]

What volume of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) gas measured at STP is evolved when \(90\text{ g}\) of glucose undergoes complete fermentation?

(Take molar mass of glucose \(= 180\text{ g mol}^{-1}\) and molar volume of gas at STP \(= 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of glucose (\(\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}\)) \(= 90\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of glucose \(= 180\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar volume of ideal gas at STP \(= 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Glucose undergoes complete conversion as per the zymase fermentation equation.
Carbon dioxide gas behaves as an ideal gas at STP.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Balanced equation: \[\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{C_2H_5OH} + 2\,\mathrm{CO_2}\]
Moles of glucose: \(n_{\text{glucose}} = \frac{m}{M}\).
Moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\): \(n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 2 \times n_{\text{glucose}}\).
Volume of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) at STP: \(V = n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \times 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate moles of glucose:
\[n_{\text{glucose}} = \frac{90\text{ g}}{180\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.50\text{ mol}\]
2. Calculate moles of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) produced:
\[n_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 2 \times 0.50\text{ mol} = 1.0\text{ mol}\]
3. Calculate volume of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) at STP:
\[V_{\mathrm{CO_2}} = 1.0\text{ mol} \times 22.4\text{ L mol}^{-1} = 22.4\text{ L}\]

Check and Final Answer:
Half a mole of glucose produces exactly one mole of \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), which occupies \(22.4\text{ L}\) at STP.
The final answer is \(22.4\text{ L}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q07 - Mass of acetone by-product in industrial phenol synthesis from cumene

questiontext.text:
Phenol is manufactured industrially from cumene (isopropylbenzene). Cumene is oxidized to cumene hydroperoxide, which on acid hydrolysis yields phenol and acetone in equimolar amounts:

\[\mathrm{C_6H_5CH(CH_3)_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{O_2}} \mathrm{C_6H_5C(CH_3)_2OOH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+/H_2O}} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\]

If an industrial plant produces \(47.0\text{ kg}\) of pure phenol, what mass of acetone is simultaneously obtained as a by-product?

(Take molar masses: Phenol \(= 94\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), Acetone \(= 58\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of phenol produced \(= 47.0\text{ kg} = 47.0 \times 10^3\text{ g}\).
Molar mass of phenol (\(\mathrm{C_6H_5OH}\)) \(= 94\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar mass of acetone (\(\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3}\)) \(= 58\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The reaction stoichiometry is strictly 1:1 between phenol and acetone as per the cumene hydroperoxide cleavage mechanism.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Mole ratio: \(1\text{ mole of cumene hydroperoxide} \rightarrow 1\text{ mole of phenol} + 1\text{ mole of acetone}\).
Therefore, moles of acetone produced \(= \text{moles of phenol produced}\).
\(n = \frac{m}{M}\); \(m_{\text{acetone}} = n \times M_{\text{acetone}}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate moles of phenol produced:
\[n_{\text{phenol}} = \frac{47.0 \times 10^3\text{ g}}{94\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 500\text{ mol}\]
2. Equate moles of acetone to moles of phenol:
\[n_{\text{acetone}} = 500\text{ mol}\]
3. Calculate mass of acetone:
\[m_{\text{acetone}} = 500\text{ mol} \times 58\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 29000\text{ g} = 29.0\text{ kg}\]

Check and Final Answer:
Mass ratio is \(\frac{58}{94} \approx 0.617\). \(47\text{ kg} \times 0.617 = 29.0\text{ kg}\). The result is verified.
The final answer is \(29.0\text{ kg}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q08 - Mass of alkyl iodides produced by ether cleavage with excess HI

questiontext.text:
When ethyl methyl ether (\(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5}\)) is heated with excess concentrated hydroiodic acid (\(\mathrm{HI}\)), it undergoes complete cleavage to form alkyl iodides according to the overall reaction:

\[\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} + 2\,\mathrm{HI} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{C_2H_5I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\]

If \(12.0\text{ g}\) of ethyl methyl ether is completely cleaved, what is the total mass of the mixture of alkyl iodides (\(\mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{C_2H_5I}\)) formed?

(Take molar masses: \(\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} = 60\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3I} = 142\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5I} = 156\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Mass of ethyl methyl ether \(= 12.0\text{ g}\).
Excess concentrated \(\mathrm{HI}\) is used with heating.
Molar masses: \(\mathrm{CH_3OC_2H_5} = 60\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{CH_3I} = 142\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), \(\mathrm{C_2H_5I} = 156\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
With excess \(\mathrm{HI}\) at elevated temperature, both the primary alkyl groups are converted into their respective alkyl iodides via nucleophilic substitution (\(\mathrm{S_N2}\)), with complete reaction yield.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Overall reaction: \[\mathrm{CH_3-O-C_2H_5} + 2\,\mathrm{HI} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH_3I} + \mathrm{C_2H_5I} + \mathrm{H_2O}\]
Moles of ether: \(n_{\text{ether}} = \frac{m_{\text{ether}}}{M_{\text{ether}}}\).
From stoichiometry, \(1\text{ mol of ether}\) produces \(1\text{ mol of } \mathrm{CH_3I}\) and \(1\text{ mol of } \mathrm{C_2H_5I}\).
Total mass of alkyl iodides: \(m_{\text{total}} = n_{\text{ether}} \times (M_{\mathrm{CH_3I}} + M_{\mathrm{C_2H_5I}})\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate moles of ethyl methyl ether:
\[n_{\text{ether}} = \frac{12.0\text{ g}}{60\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.20\text{ mol}\]
2. Calculate moles of each alkyl iodide formed:
\[n_{\mathrm{CH_3I}} = 0.20\text{ mol}\]
\[n_{\mathrm{C_2H_5I}} = 0.20\text{ mol}\]
3. Calculate individual masses:
\[m_{\mathrm{CH_3I}} = 0.20\text{ mol} \times 142\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 28.4\text{ g}\]
\[m_{\mathrm{C_2H_5I}} = 0.20\text{ mol} \times 156\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 31.2\text{ g}\]
4. Calculate total mass of alkyl iodides:
\[m_{\text{total}} = 28.4\text{ g} + 31.2\text{ g} = 59.6\text{ g}\]

Check and Final Answer:
Combined molar mass of the two iodides is \(142 + 156 = 298\text{ g mol}^{-1}\). For \(0.20\text{ mol}\), total mass \(= 0.20 \times 298 = 59.6\text{ g}\). The calculation is verified.
The final answer is \(59.6\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q09 - Mass of diborane required in hydroboration oxidation of propene

questiontext.text:
Propan-1-ol is prepared from propene via hydroboration-oxidation according to the sequence:

\[6\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{B_2H_6} \rightarrow 2\,(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2})_3\mathrm{B}\]\[(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2})_3\mathrm{B} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2O_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}} 3\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH} + \mathrm{B(OH)_3}\]

What is the minimum mass of diborane (\(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)) required to synthesize \(36.0\text{ g}\) of propan-1-ol with an overall yield of \(80\%\)?

(Take molar masses: Propan-1-ol \(= 60.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\), Diborane \(= 27.6\text{ g mol}^{-1}\))

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
Actual mass of propan-1-ol produced \(= 36.0\text{ g}\).
Overall reaction yield \(= 80\%\).
Molar mass of propan-1-ol (\(\mathrm{C_3H_7OH}\)) \(= 60.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).
Molar mass of diborane (\(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\)) \(= 27.6\text{ g mol}^{-1}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
Diborane behaves as a dimer equivalent to two \(\mathrm{BH_3}\) units, each adding three alkene molecules to form trialkylborane.
The overall stoichiometric ratio between diborane and the alcohol product is determined from the coupled sequence.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
Combining both stages of the sequence:
\[6\,\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2} + \mathrm{B_2H_6} + 6\,\mathrm{H_2O_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}} 6\,\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2OH} + 2\,\mathrm{B(OH)_3}\]
Stoichiometric ratio: \(1\text{ mol of } \mathrm{B_2H_6}\) produces \(6\text{ moles of propan-1-ol}\).
Theoretical yield of propan-1-ol \(= \frac{\text{Actual mass}}{\text{Percentage yield}}\).
Required moles of diborane: \(n_{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} = \frac{n_{\text{alcohol (theoretical)}}}{6}\).
Mass of diborane: \(m_{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} = n_{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} \times M_{\mathrm{B_2H_6}}\).

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate actual moles of propan-1-ol produced:
\[n_{\text{actual}} = \frac{36.0\text{ g}}{60.0\text{ g mol}^{-1}} = 0.60\text{ mol}\]
2. Calculate theoretical moles of propan-1-ol required:
\[n_{\text{theoretical}} = \frac{0.60\text{ mol}}{0.80} = 0.75\text{ mol}\]
3. From stoichiometry, calculate moles of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) required:
\[n_{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} = \frac{0.75\text{ mol}}{6} = 0.125\text{ mol}\]
4. Calculate required mass of diborane:
\[m_{\mathrm{B_2H_6}} = 0.125\text{ mol} \times 27.6\text{ g mol}^{-1} = 3.45\text{ g}\]

Check and Final Answer:
At 100% yield, \(0.10\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{B_2H_6}\) (\(2.76\text{ g}\)) would give \(0.60\text{ mol}\) of alcohol. Accounting for the 80% yield, \(\frac{2.76\text{ g}}{0.80} = 3.45\text{ g}\). The calculation is verified.
The final answer is \(3.45\text{ g}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ALCOHOLS_PHENOLS_AND_ETHERS_NUMERICAL_Q10 - Ratio of acid dissociation constants of o-nitrophenol and phenol

questiontext.text:
According to NCERT Table 7.3, the \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) values of o-nitrophenol and phenol are \(7.2\) and \(10.0\) respectively at \(298\text{ K}\).

By what factor is the acid dissociation constant (\(K_a\)) of o-nitrophenol greater than that of phenol?

generalfeedback.text:
Given Data and Conditions:
\(\mathrm{p}K_a \text{ of o-nitrophenol} = 7.2\).
\(\mathrm{p}K_a \text{ of phenol} = 10.0\).
Temperature \(T = 298\text{ K}\).

Assumptions and Sign Conventions:
The definition of \(\mathrm{p}K_a\) is \(\mathrm{p}K_a = -\log_{10}(K_a)\).
The ratio of dissociation constants represents relative acid strength.

Relevant Formulae and Principles:
\[K_a = 10^{-\mathrm{p}K_a}\]
The ratio of the acid dissociation constant of o-nitrophenol (\(K_{a1}\)) to that of phenol (\(K_{a2}\)) is:
\[\frac{K_{a1}}{K_{a2}} = \frac{10^{-\mathrm{p}K_{a1}}}{10^{-\mathrm{p}K_{a2}}} = 10^{\mathrm{p}K_{a2} - \mathrm{p}K_{a1}}\]

Step-by-Step Working:
1. Calculate the difference in \(\mathrm{p}K_a\):
\[\Delta \mathrm{p}K_a = \mathrm{p}K_a(\text{phenol}) - \mathrm{p}K_a(\text{o-nitrophenol}) = 10.0 - 7.2 = 2.8\]
2. Express the factor as a power of 10:
\[\frac{K_{a1}}{K_{a2}} = 10^{2.8} = 10^{2 + 0.8} = 10^2 \times 10^{0.8} = 100 \times 10^{0.8}\]
3. Compute \(10^{0.8}\):
Since \(\log_{10}(2) \approx 0.3010\), \(\log_{10}(6.31) \approx 0.800\):
\[10^{0.8} \approx 6.31\]
4. Multiply by 100:
\[100 \times 6.31 = 631\]

Check and Final Answer:
Since \(10^{2.8}\) lies between \(10^2 = 100\) and \(10^3 = 1000\), and \(10^{2.5} \approx 316\), \(10^{2.8} \approx 631\) is mathematically accurate.
The final answer is \(631\).
